records.name: Cyprus
records.current_summary:
Cyprus is workable for trans visitors. The legal framework is mid-transition: public incitement to hatred based on gender identity is a criminal offence (2015), and gender identity is an aggravating factor in hate crime (2017). A legal gender recognition bill (self-determination basis) was approved by the Council of Ministers in September 2022 and is pending in parliament; until it passes, LGR requires surgery under the 2002 Civil Registry Law — a resident-facing gap.

No traveler-facing restrictions: no bathroom law, no border issues (EU member), tourist infrastructure is Western-standard and accustomed to diverse visitors. Gender identity is not yet an explicit ground in the non-discrimination framework, and the divided island matters: the northern part (de facto Turkish-controlled) has its own LGR regime requiring surgical proof, weaker protections, and less documentation — travelers should treat the north as closer to Turkey's risk profile.
records.current_localsOnly: The pending self-determination LGR bill and the current surgery requirement under the 2002 Civil Registry Law are resident-facing.
records.current_outOfScope: The north/south division and pending LGR bill are noted; LGR requirements are resident-facing.

sources.claim: UPR-info Cyprus advocacy sheet (2024): Law 87(I)/2015 criminalises public incitement to violence/hatred on SOGI grounds; Law 31(I)/2017 makes prejudice motivation an aggravating sentencing factor; Law 39(I)/2023 bans and criminalises conversion practices; the legal gender recognition bill was approved by the Council of Ministers Sept 2022 with first parliamentary reading Nov 2022 (still pending at 2024); gender identity remains absent from equal-treatment grounds and no anti-homophobia action plan exists; prison guards received 2-day LGBTI+ training (Apr 2023) after anti-LGBTI harassment complaints to the Ombudswoman.

European Commission Network of Legal Experts country report on gender equality in Cyprus (2024, reporting period 2023): how EU equality rules are transposed into Cypriot national law, including gender-identity-related aspects of the legal framework.

Queer Cyprus Association UPR presentation (Erman Dolmacı, 4th-cycle): confirms the same three Criminal Code amendments (87(I)/2015 incitement, 31(I)/2017 aggravating factor, 39(I)/2023 conversion-practices ban), frames 'ISSUE 1' as trans and gender-diverse rights with the Sept 2022 LGR bill as the outstanding implementation step, and lists the state response to prior UPR recommendations — i.e. hate-speech law delivered, gender-identity discrimination ground and trans legislation not yet delivered.

Queer Cyprus 'Diversity of Colours' LGR booklet: documents gender-recognition practice on the divided island — the record's framework is self-determination without psychiatric or surgical gatekeeping ('no psychiatric involvement'), and the northern part of Cyprus runs its own recognition process, explicitly including recognition of non-binary identities. Practical resource: Queer Cyprus runs a 7-days/week confidential psychosocial and legal support line covering identity, work, family, shelter, health and military-service issues.

ILGA 32nd UPR session report (29 Jan 2019): Cyprus received 8 SOGIESC recommendations and accepted all 8; national report stated new legislation for correcting registered sex (adults and minors) was in preparation requiring only a Registrar decision, no prior medical intervention or psychiatric reports; ECRI had urged gender identity as a prohibited discrimination ground; Cyprus joined the Equal Rights Coalition as 40th member (Aug 2018). Marks the reform promise the 2022 bill was meant to fulfil.

European Commission legal experts' country report on non-discrimination in Cyprus (2020, reporting period 2019): transposition and implementation of the EU equality directives, including SOGI grounds in Cypriot law.

PinkNews (10 Oct 2013): Cyprus amended its penal code to criminalise incitement to violence or hatred based on sexual orientation or gender identity, punishable by up to 3 years' imprisonment and/or a €5,000 fine (workplace SOGI protections added 2004). Dated, still-accurate baseline for the hate-speech offence the 2015 law extended.

freshness_all.fact: Decriminalised 1998, civil unions since 2015, conversion therapy since banned; the 2013 penal-code source remains accurate as background.

records.name: Cambodia
records.current_summary:
Cambodia is workable for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised — Cambodia has never criminalised same-sex activity or gender expression — and the government is formally cooperative: it accepted all 12 SOGIESC recommendations at its 2024 Universal Periodic Review, including legal gender recognition, and hosted the UN Independent Expert on SOGI in 2023. Phnom Penh and Siem Reap have visible trans communities and tourist infrastructure accustomed to diverse visitors.

The risks are street-level and police-level rather than legal: the Cambodian Centre for Human Rights documents “shocking” harassment and abuse of transgender women in urban centres, including a reported Siem Reap police practice of targeting trans women (extortion and abuse). There is no legal gender recognition yet, no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and no hate-crime statute.

For a visitor: low probability of legal trouble; moderate probability of harassment if visibly trans outside tourist areas; police are a risk factor, not a protection, for trans women especially.
records.current_localsOnly: The LGR absence and discrimination-law gaps are resident-facing; the Siem Reap police extortion practice primarily affects resident trans women.
records.current_outOfScope: LGR absence and discrimination-law gaps are resident-facing.

sources.claim: UN in Cambodia page for the UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity visit report: identifies good practices and remaining challenges and formulates recommendations to strengthen protection against violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity; an unofficial Khmer translation was prepared for national stakeholders.

OutRight International Cambodia profile (updated 12 Mar 2026): Cambodia has never criminalised same-sex sexual activity (French protectorate 1867, independence 1953); at UPR 2019 accepted recommendations to legalise same-sex marriage and at UPR 2024 accepted all 12 LGBTIQ recommendations incl. seven on marriage equality; legislation contains no SOGI non-discrimination provisions.

Phnom Penh Post on a Cambodian Centre for Human Rights (CCHR) report: an overwhelming majority of transgender women on Cambodia's city streets face 'shocking' harassment and abuse (135+ cases documented), including a disturbing Siem Reap police practice of targeting transgender sex workers and forcing them to bathe in dirty, stagnant river water.

Rainbow Community Kampuchea (RoCK) page on Cambodia's 4th-cycle UPR: Cambodia officially accepted all 12 SOGIESC/LGBT+ recommendations in 2024 - marriage equality progress, legal gender recognition for self-defined identity, and anti-discrimination measures; includes the civil-society joint submission (Dec 2023) and summary factsheets.

UNDP/USAID 'Being LGBT in Asia: Cambodia Country Report' (2014): participatory review of the legal and social environment for LGBT persons and civil society, based on the Cambodia National LGBT Community Dialogue (Phnom Penh, Jan 2013), participant conversations, an NGO/CBO survey and a desk review of published literature.
Frommer's travel guide: 'Tips for Gay and Lesbian Travelers' in Cambodia - practical travel advice for LGBT visitors (page largely navigation content at fetch time).

PinkNews (20 Jul 2019) on Rainbow Community Kampuchea (RoCK) study: 81% of queer women and transgender people under 35 suffered emotional abuse by a family member; 35% of under-35 participants considered suicide because of family rejection — including a 27-year-old trans man forced by his mother into rehab to 'fix his gender'.

records.name: Nepal
records.current_summary:
Nepal is workable for trans visitors — South Asia's most legally recognising country. The Supreme Court has protected gender identity since the landmark 2007 Sunil Babu Pant decision; a third-gender “O” category exists on documents by self-identification; and in 2024 the Supreme Court ruled (Rukshana Kapali case) that a trans woman must be recognised as female without medical verification. Nothing is criminalised, and Kathmandu has an established activist scene (Blue Diamond Society, founded 2001).

The gap between doctrine and practice is large: HRW documents (“We Have to Beg So Many People,” 2024) that implementation is piecemeal and humiliating, and trans people in provinces like Madhesh face physical and sexual harassment in public spaces with little police protection. These burdens fall overwhelmingly on residents navigating citizenship documents — a visitor with a foreign passport faces none of the bureaucratic gauntlet.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, tolerant tourist areas, but expect stares and possible harassment if visibly trans outside Kathmandu/Pokhara bubbles.
records.current_localsOnly: The third-gender “O” category, the Rukshana Kapali ruling, and the HRW-documented implementation failures all concern residents navigating citizenship documents.
records.current_outOfScope: Documentation barriers are resident-facing; citizenship-law discrimination does not affect visitors.

sources.claim: HRW (Feb 2024): calls on Nepal's government to urgently create a clear, simple, rights-respecting procedure so transgender and third-gender people can obtain official documents — illustrating that despite progressive rulings, no straightforward document-change process exists (photo shows a Kathmandu trans woman holding her 2023 citizenship certificate listing female gender). For this record: official-observer statement on the documentary-recognition gap.

JURIST (Aug 2024): Nepal's Supreme Court ruled that trans law student Rukshana Kapali must be legally recognised as a woman on all documents without medical verification, after she filed 50+ lawsuits since 2021; changing markers to 'female'/'male' has usually required surgery abroad plus in-country medical evaluations including intrusive post-operative genital exams. For this record: the landmark ruling and the pre-ruling barrier path, dated.

The Diplomat (Feb 2024): Nepal's 2007 ruling allowing self-identified legal gender was novel at the time and later cases reinforced it, but government officials limited changes to people identifying as 'third gender' while male/female marker changes lagged — the country's progressive reputation outruns policy. For this record: documented doctrine-versus-implementation gap.

Kathmandu Post feature (Nov 2024) on trans life in Janakpur: trans people face discrimination in public spaces and in government institutions and are often subjected to physical and sexual harassment. For this record: ground-level conditions for visibly trans people in provincial cities, dated 2024.

APTN (Asia Pacific Transgender Network) publication (Oct 2021, in Nepali): 'Gender Identity Draft Bill 2078: Civil Society Proposal' - by Rukshana Kapali and Allan Bhandari with advocate Subin Mulmi, produced through the Amplifying Trans Advocacy Fellowship; a civil-society draft bill on legal gender recognition in Nepal.

The Record (Sept 25, 2020) by Queer Youth Group and Queer Rights Collective: argues that despite the Constitution awarding the right to self-determine name and gender markers (2007 case), 'an extensive overhaul of the law and the language of the law' is still needed to address inequalities faced by the trans and broader PoMSOGIESC community. For this record: local-activist assessment of the gap between constitutional right and statute.

SIT Study Abroad ISP (Spring 2015) by Sophia Greene: 'Gender and Sexuality in Nepal: The Experiences of Sexual and Gender Minorities in a Rapidly Changing Social Climate' - despite changing legislation, sexual and gender minorities face deeply rooted stigma and obstacles in virtually every arena of life amid the clash of patriarchal tradition and modernisation.

records.name: Mongolia
records.current_summary:
Mongolia is workable for trans visitors. Same-sex activity was decriminalised in 1993, discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited, and SOGI was added to the hate-crime provisions of the Criminal Code in 2015. Legal gender recognition exists via a medicalised process, and Ulaanbaatar has an organised community (LGBT Centre) that successfully lobbied for these protections.

Counterweights: protections are fragmented (no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering all areas), the LGBT Centre has documented periods of elevated hate speech and assaults — including attacks on its own staff — and social acceptance outside the capital is low. There are no bathroom laws, no border/document friction for foreign passports, and no police targeting pattern; the realistic risk is street harassment if visibly trans, particularly at night and outside central Ulaanbaatar.
records.current_localsOnly: The medicalised LGR process and the fragmented anti-discrimination protections are resident-facing; the LGBT Centre assault documentation describes residents' experience.
records.current_outOfScope: Comprehensive anti-discrimination gaps and medicalised LGR are resident-facing.

sources.claim: Outright International (last updated 12 March 2026): consensual same-sex intimacy decriminalised 1993; sexual-orientation and gender-identity discrimination prohibited but protections fragmented (no comprehensive law); marriage equality constitutionally prohibited with no union recognition; groups can register.
thin: no usable finding

The Establishment (Aug 2018): profiles Anaraa Nyamdorj, trans man and co-founder/advisor of the LGBT Centre — came out in 2004, began transition in 2011; describes Mongolia's 2018 Pride and LGBT Centre advocacy; ground on trans life, transition access and acceptance in Ulaanbaatar.

Al Jazeera (Oct 2019): after an officer assaulted a detained transgender woman, the LGBT Center trained police on the 2017 criminal code's hate-crime provisions — 500+ police officers, prosecutors and judges trained; force now has guidelines requiring officers to address transgender detainees by their identified gender regardless of ID documents.

GlobalGayz Mongolia report: no laws specifically against homosexuality though 'satisfaction of immoral sexual needs' provisions remain; the scene has virtually no presence, venues or activism; a 2008 account describes two organisations holding furtive monthly parties where attendees fear being outed.

records.name: Ecuador
records.current_summary:
Ecuador demands real caution from trans visitors — a country whose legal framework is now among Latin America's strongest while its streets are among the region's most dangerous. Legal gender recognition has existed since 2016; the 2024 Organic Law reform lets adults change name and sex/gender on the ID card directly through the Civil Registry (one time, no surgery); and in 2024-25 Constitutional Court rulings extended document changes to trans adolescents and reprimanded the Assembly for stalling trans-rights implementation.

The violence side is severe: Runa Sipiy documented 27 LGBTQ+ people murdered in 2023, with inadequate state response, and the “internal armed conflict” against gangs has intensified general violence since January 2024 — two more LGBTQ people killed in its first weeks. Quito and Guayaquil carry real street risk, and police capacity is consumed by the security crisis.

For a visitor: documents and expression are legally protected, but the probability of encountering violence if outed in public is among the highest in South America right now.
records.current_localsOnly: The 2024 Civil Registry reform and the adolescent document-change rulings are resident-facing; the 27-murder toll and its inadequate state response fall on residents.
records.current_outOfScope: The general security emergency affects all travelers; the score reflects the trans-specific legal/violence balance.

sources.claim: Primicias (12 Jun 2024): President Noboa issued on 11 Jun 2024 the reglamento to the National Assembly's 12 Dec 2023 reforms of the Organic Law on Identity Management and Civil Data, streamlining civil-registry gender-marker changes — the operative procedure for legal gender recognition.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Los Angeles Blade piece (Jan 2024) reports violence against LGBTQ Ecuadorians increasing amid the internal armed conflict.
AP (Apr 2026): 'A transgender teen's case in Ecuador opens path for others seeking legal recognition' — Constitutional Court rulings let trans adolescents change name and sex on official records.

Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex marriage legalised in 2019 but same-sex couples barred from adoption by constitutional ban; legal gender recognition possible since 2016 (not available to under-18s); conversion practices involving torture are explicitly criminalised.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Ecuador: documents discrimination based on sexual orientation among societal problems, alongside excessive police force, media restrictions and corruption - baseline context.

2008 Constitution of Ecuador (Georgetown/PDBA text): Article 11 principles bind the state to respect ethnic, national, social, generational and gender differences and sexual orientation and identity — the constitutional non-discrimination foundation for LGBTI rights in a secular, multinational state.

PinkNews (31 May 2018): the Constitutional Court ordered the Civil Registry to register the daughter of same-sex couple Helen Bicknell and Nicola Rothon (child Satya Amani Bicknell Rothon); lawyer Jose Luis Guerra said refusal violated the child's rights — a precedent ordering state recognition of same-sex families.

records.name: Jordan
records.current_summary:
Jordan demands real caution from trans visitors — the safest of the Levantine Arab states by a clear margin, but on a deteriorating trajectory. Same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 1951, and courts have granted legal gender recognition in individual cases (the 2014 Court of Cassation ruling — though justified by reclassifying the plaintiff as intersex). There is no statute criminalising gender expression itself.

The deterioration is documented: Cairo 52 reports a notable rise in targeting of transgender individuals and spaces by both security forces and civilians, using Ottoman/British-era morality laws; Jordanian security forces coerced queer community spaces into complete cessation of activities; the 2023 cybercrime law (“inciting immorality”) gives authorities a digital tool against LGBT expression; and gender-affirming surgery is criminalised for trans people (Article 8, Medical and Health Liability Law) while permitted for intersex people. In 2021 security forces arrested 14 people at a private party.

For a visitor: no legal exposure for gender expression per se, but morality-law discretion, shuttered community infrastructure, and family-society hostility make outing dangerous.
records.current_localsOnly: The criminalisation of gender-affirming surgery (Article 8) and the case-by-case LGR rulings are resident-facing.
records.current_outOfScope: Surgery criminalisation and LGR case law are resident-facing; morality-law and cybercrime enforcement are the traveler-relevant mechanisms.

sources.claim: CAIRO 52 Jordan country profile: new legislation curtails LGBTQ+ speech and digital access; security forces coerced queer community spaces into closing, pushing transgender and queer people to leave; intersex people can change legal gender markers but transgender people cannot, and gender-affirming healthcare is penalised for providers under medical-liability law.

OutRight International Jordan profile (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations are NOT criminalised — Jordan abolished the colonial-era ban in 1951; no clear legal pathway for trans people to change gender markers (allowed 'in some cases'); gender-affirming surgery permitted for intersex people but criminalised for transgender people under Article 8 of the Medical and Health Liability Law (25) of 2018.

HRW World Report 2024 Jordan chapter (11 Jan 2024): authorities limited civic space in 2023 and enacted a new cybercrime law undermining free speech and privacy online; peaceful dissidents and journalists arrested and harassed under vague, abusive laws, with intrusive digital surveillance — the environment shaping online expression for visitors and locals alike.

CAIRO 52 analysis of Case No. 2092/2014 (Jordan): Jordanian legislation criminalises sex reassignment with penalties up to 10 years' imprisonment (except intersex cases); the plaintiff (born 1977) sought name and gender change from male to female in official records after undergoing hormone therapy and surgery in Australia, since such procedures are unavailable domestically.

HRW (6 Jun 2024): in Egypt, Jordan and Kuwait, same-sex relations are not explicitly criminalised in some, yet authorities 'legally' harass LGBT people via public-morality and debauchery laws — alternative legal avenues substitute for formal criminalisation, so decriminalisation on paper does not equal safety.

HRW report (April 2018) 'Audacity in Adversity': LGBT activism in the Middle East and North Africa - despite state-sponsored repression and stigma, LGBT people are speaking out, building alliances and regional movements; includes an annex of laws used to punish same-sex conduct and gender expression across MENA (Jordan among them).

HRW (4 Dec 2023): Jordanian authorities systematically targeted LGBT rights activists in a coordinated crackdown on free expression and assembly around gender and sexuality; officials smeared activists online by sexual orientation and social-media users posted their photos with messages inciting violence — two LGBT organisation directors cited official intimidation.

records.name: Venezuela
records.current_summary:
Venezuela demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing about gender expression is criminalised, but Venezuela has achieved no meaningful legal recognition for LGBTIQ+ people: no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, no hate-crime statute. Since the disputed July 2024 election, activists document unprecedented persecution of the LGBTQ community amid the broader repression wave, and arbitrary detention powers are used broadly against perceived dissidents.

Caracas has a small visible scene, and trans women have historically been a visible part of urban life, but the economic collapse means healthcare (including HRT access) is severely degraded, police are predatory toward everyone, and there is no institutional recourse. The risk profile for a visitor is less about trans-specific targeting and more about the combination of zero legal protection, arbitrary state power, and high general violence.
records.current_localsOnly: The degraded healthcare including HRT access is resident-facing; the post-2024 persecution wave primarily affects resident activists and communities.
records.current_outOfScope: General humanitarian and repression context affects all travelers; the score reflects the trans-specific protection vacuum.

sources.claim: Washington Blade (10 Sep 2024): LGBTQ Venezuelans face unprecedented persecution after the disputed July 2024 election; the opposition presidential candidate fled the country on 7 Sep 2024 -- persecution of LGBTQ people tied to the political crisis, dated.

EUAA asylum country-focus (reference period through 2025): dedicated LGBTIQ+ profile of conditions in Venezuela used for international protection decisions -- the EU asylum agency's factual baseline on how LGBTIQ+ people are treated.
NOTE: The AFS/Vance Center LGBTQ guide on Venezuela (Oct 2024) returned no extractable text at fetch time (image-based PDF).

Sydney Morning Herald (8 Aug 2015): Tamara Adrian, Venezuela's first transgender candidate, ran for the National Assembly -- landmark trans political candidacy under Venezuela's gender-recognition law context.

Cronica Uno poll (2-3 Mar 2023): a majority of Venezuelans agree the LGBTIQ population should have the same rights as other citizens; 82% know the LGBTIQ+ term (13% do not); 36% think gay/lesbian/bisexuality is innate -- dated public-opinion data.

Blog record (31 Jan 2014): an equal-marriage bill was set to be presented to Venezuela's National Assembly that week (per Aporrea) -- legislative push for same-sex marriage, historic milestone (no later enactment recorded).

El Mundo (13 Dec 2015): Amnesty International declared Rosmit Mantilla -- Voluntad Popular deputy and Venezuela's first openly gay parliamentarian -- a prisoner of conscience held in SEBIN custody; he turned 33 in his cell -- state persecution of an openly gay politician.

records.name: Bolivia
records.current_summary:
Bolivia is workable for trans visitors — one of Latin America's legal pioneers on paper. The 2016 Gender Identity Law was ground-breaking: legal gender recognition on the basis of self-declared identity (administrative process, no surgery), and gender identity is an explicitly protected ground in anti-discrimination law. Bolivia's constitution also names gender identity.

Implementation lags the statute: the first national LGBTQ+ survey (2024) reveals significant exclusion in health, education, employment, and housing; social conservatism is strong outside La Paz/Santa Cruz; and bureaucrats often resist applying the Gender Identity Law. There is no documented pattern of police targeting of trans people as such, and no traveler-facing restriction — but also limited effective protection outside major cities.
records.current_localsOnly: The Gender Identity Law's administrative process, and its uneven implementation by bureaucrats, are resident-facing; the 2024 survey exclusion data describes residents' lives.
records.current_outOfScope: LGR mechanics and discrimination-law enforcement gaps are resident-facing.

sources.claim: Comparative Politics article (April 2024) 'Activists, Parties, and the Expansion of Trans Rights in Bolivia': Bolivia prohibits gender-identity discrimination and passed a ground-breaking gender identity law (2016, allowing name/marker change) despite low voter support; trans activists leveraged access to ruling-party legislators; contradictory heteronormative laws passed alongside because both organised religion and LGBT activists were party constituents.

NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (WordPress critical error); the underlying Agencia Presentes article (Dec 2024) covers Bolivia's first virtual survey revealing the great exclusion of LGBTI people.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Bolivia: general human-rights assessment (arbitrary deprivation of life, prison conditions, corruption) - the LGBT section documents the constitutional anti-discrimination guarantee and societal discrimination.

Newsweek (Jul 2017): after the US trans military ban, only 18 countries are believed to fully legalise LGBT military service — international baseline for whether trans visitors/soldiers face service exclusion; Bolivia not singled out in the text.

Legal-profile page: Constitution prohibits discrimination and guarantees bodily integrity (Art 15(II) violence, 45(V) maternity), Penal Code Title VIII governs abortion. Superseded by post-2016 law: 2016 gender-identity law (self-ID), Jan-2018 Inter-American Court opinion, Dec-2020 civil-registry 'free union' recognition for same-sex couples.

eju.tv/La Razón (25 Aug 2014, Spanish): homosexuality is taboo in Bolivia's armed forces — gay soldiers report discrimination and sanctions, testimony given anonymously; the TLGB collective and human-rights activists demand openness.

freshness_all.fact: Post-2017 developments the archived sources miss: Jan-2018 Inter-American Court opinion; Dec-2020 civil-registry 'free union' recognition; 2016 gender-identity law remains a world-leading baseline. 2024 article still current.
